Optimize L-BFGS-B with efficient LU factorization

Replace explicit matrix inversion (M_) with cached LU factorization
(MM_lu_) for more efficient triangular solves. This reduces numerical
instability and improves computational performance when solving linear
systems during optimization steps.

Add point projection to handle infeasible initial points by clipping
to bounds before gradient computation. Introduce conditional line search
that skips when Cauchy point is already optimal (no free variables).

Improve numerical stability by using fixed epsilon (1e-12) instead of
machine epsilon and refactor curvature check with clearer naming (sTy).

Update SubspaceMinimization to return both the solution and a flag
indicating whether line search is needed, enabling early termination
when the Cauchy point is optimal. Replace all M_ * v operations with
SolveM(v) calls using the cached LU factorization.

Implement constrained optimization and improve L-BFGS

This commit introduces support for constrained optimization problems
and improves the L-BFGS algorithm.

All functions will receive the position to evaluate and return an entire
state (x, f(x), grad*, hessian*) instead of treating them separately.
This simplifies the interface, while template parameters take care of
treating functions according their differentiability.

To support constrained problems, a new solver is implemented which can
wrap all existing solvers to solver the unconstrained
one via penalty method and augmented Lagrangian.

It supports now:
  min  f(x)
  s.t. c1(x) >= 0
       c2(x)  = 0

Several changes are made to L-BFGS for more robust numerical handling of
edge-cases.

Use the seed supplied to user-facing functions to generate new seeds for

downstream code on-the-fly.

The approach implemented now changes the default of `seed` (and `.seed`) arguments from `NULL` to `sample.int(.Machine$integer.max, 1)`. For top-level functions which are only called by the user and not within projpred (should only be `cv_varsel()`, `project()`, and `proj_predict()`), this is not strictly necessary, but done for consistency with lower-level functions which are also called within projpred.

The main advantage of generating seeds on-the-fly is that more seeds may be easily added and used in downstream code (which will be important for fixing issue #268), without always having to add a new argument to top-level functions. Apart from that, this approach makes it possible that users set a seed once at the beginning of their script and then use the default `seed` (and `.seed`) arguments -- they will then get reproducible results which would not have been the case for the former implementation.

However, due to the resetting of `.Random.seed`, this approach does not avoid yet that the same seed is re-used multiple times (which is probably bad practice from a theoretical point of view).

`plot.vsel()`: Minor efficiency enhancement concerning the two `.tabulate_stats()` calls in lines

```
tab <- rbind(
  .tabulate_stats(object, stats, alpha = alpha,
nfeat_baseline = nfeat_baseline, resp_oscale = resp_oscale,
...),
  .tabulate_stats(object, stats, alpha = alpha, resp_oscale = resp_oscale, ...)
)
stats_table <- subset(tab, tab$delta == deltas)
```

This simplification is possible because `nfeat_baseline` (resulting from
`get_nfeat_baseline()`) is always non-`NULL` at these lines, meaning that within
the first of these two `.tabulate_stats()` calls, `delta` is `TRUE` and in the
second of these two `.tabulate_stats()` calls, `delta` is `FALSE`. Therefore,
`subset(tab, tab$delta == deltas)` picks the rows from the first of the two
`.tabulate_stats()` calls if `deltas` is `TRUE` and the rows from the second of
the two `.tabulate_stats()` calls if `deltas` is `FALSE`.

This simplification also avoids an unnecessary second message in case of the
latent projection with `resp_oscale = FALSE`, `stat %in% c("elpd", "mlpd")` and
`<refmodel>$dis` consisting only of `NA`s.

KL divergence aggregation across observations for the `gaussian()` family: Replace

sum by mean (because in `.init_submodel()`, `pseudo_data()$wobs` simply returns
`weights` in that case and those `weights` are not normalized anymore since PR
198). The use of the sum should have had no consequences, though, because in the
currently used KL divergence for the Gaussian family, other constants are
dropped anyway, so dropping 1/N (with N denoting the number of observations) as
another constant shouldn't have done any harm. However, it's probably better to
be explicit and replace the sum by the mean, especially because in the future,
the exact KL divergence might be implemented for the Gaussian family (which
should be achievable by not regarding the dispersion parameter (the residual
standard deviation) as another constant and by not dropping any constants) and
then this aggregation across the observations would already be prepared.

Alternatively, one could have re-introduced the normalization of the observation
weights (i.e., partly reverting PR #198), but for the `binomial()` family,
unnormalized weights indeed make more sense from a theoretical point of view, so
use unnormalized weights for consistency of all families. (The sum of the
observation weights is again a constant, so it shouldn't matter much anyway,
except for the rare case that a user wants to extract the KL divergences without
any constants dropped, but as explained above, for the Gaussian family, other
constants are currently dropped anyway.)

important fix for the projection for non Gaussian models:

When we want to project a non gaussian model we solve least squares on a pseudo
gaussian transformation of the expected value of the reference model. This is
currently handled by a surrogate MLE solver such as lme4. Nonetheless, we need
to recompute the approximation at every iteration of the least squares
algorithm. Given that we don't have access to the inner workings of lme4 and we
cannot provide a full custom link function (because we miss the inverse), i have
coded a simple  but ugly surrogate that iterates an MLE solution replacing the
target after every iteration with the new computation. This needs further work
and testing. It seems to work but for instance for a poisson model there are
some bad submodels that I need to look into in more detail.

change consists of the possibility of different results since the PRNG state
when generating the CV folds would be a different one when using the new default
of `seed = NA` in `cv_folds()` (so the folds could be composed differently).

Using `seed = sample.int(.Machine$integer.max, 1)` in this special `cv_folds()`
call should not be a problem as the PRNG state that `cv_folds()` resets to upon
exit is never used again for generating a seed. (After this special `cv_folds()`

construction can be avoided in the feature when introducing other breaking
changes (e.g., in an upcoming UI overhaul).

Normalize the observation-aggregated KL divergence by

the sum of the observation weights, not by the number of observations. This
makes more sense for the binomial family with > 1 trials (because there,
observations with more trials should probably be given more weight in the
aggregated KL divergence). The fact that in case of the binomial and the Poisson
family, `family$dev.resids()` now receives normalized weights should just be
considered as a technical trick to avoid dividing the S columns of its output by
the normalization constant (and divide the N (usually N << S) observation
weights by the normalization constant instead).

Again, this just affects the normalization constant of the aggregated KL
divergence, so it shouldn't matter much anyway, except for the rare case that a
user wants to extract the KL divergences without any constants dropped, but for
the Gaussian family, other constants are currently dropped anyway.

Fix issue #242 (#253)

* Fix issue #242 (Refactors and bugs in `.init_submodel()`), i.e., perform the

following modifications simultaneously:

* Remove a comment which seems to be a remnant from older code.
* Don't define object `weights` (not necessary).
* Rename `ref` to `p_ref`.
* Simplify `.init_submodel()` for the Gaussian family. (For the `gaussian()`
family with `f = 0`, the following holds within `pseudo_data()`:
    + `family$linkinv(f + offset)` is equal to `offset`.
    + `family$mu.eta()` gives all-ones.
    + `family$variance()` gives all-ones.

    Therefore, `z <- f + (y - mu) / dmu_df` is equivalent to `z <- y - offset`.
Furthermore, `wobs <- (weights * dmu_df^2) / family$variance(mu)` is equivalent
to `wobs <- weights`.)
* Fix a wrong handling of offsets for the Gaussian family: The final `ref$mu`
had offsets subtracted twice (compared to the point where they were originally
included once, namely in `posterior_linpred()`) whereas the submodel's `mu`
includes them (once).
* Fix a wrong handling of offsets for non-Gaussian families: The final `ref$mu`
had offsets subtracted (compared to the point where they were originally
included, namely in `posterior_linpred()`) whereas the submodel's `mu` includes
them.
* Add an error for the `Student_t()` family (because in `family$dis_fun(ref,
nlist(mu), ref$wobs)`, `ref$wobs` was `NULL` in that case, so `/ sum(wobs)` in
`dis_student_t()` divided by 0).

* Add test for `pseudo_data(f = 0, [...], family = extend_family(gaussian()), [...])`.

is glm performing iterative least squares?

in theory we fit a gaussian approximation to the non gaussian
observation model by computing pseudo gaussian transformations of the
log likelihood and fitting a Gaussian model instead. Nonetheless, using
lm in the internal iteration returns a much worse approximation than
using glm, but that should be the theoretically correct approach?

The algorithm as I picture it should look like

1. compute pseudo gaussian observation z_i and weights w_i.
2. perform one iteration of weighted least squares with z_i as
target (this approximates a gaussian to the regression coefficients)
3. go back to 1 replacing the current guess with the link prediction of
the previous guess until convergence.

Check for `NA`s in `d_test`. Illustration:

```
data("df_gaussian", package = "projpred")
df_gaussian_train <- df_gaussian[1:80, ]
df_gaussian_test <- df_gaussian[81:100, ]
dat_train <- data.frame(y = df_gaussian_train$y, df_gaussian_train$x)
dat_test <- data.frame(y = df_gaussian_test$y, df_gaussian_test$x)
dat_test[4, "X3"] <- NA
library(rstanarm)
rfit <- stan_glm(y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5,
                 data = dat_train,
                 chains = 1,
                 iter = 500,
                 seed = 1140350788,
                 refresh = 0)
library(projpred)
vs <- varsel(
  rfit,
  d_test = list(
    data = dat_test[, names(dat_test) != "y"],
    offset = rep(0, nrow(dat_test)),
    weights = rep(1, nrow(dat_test)),
    y = dat_test[["y"]]
  ),
  nclusters = 3,
  nclusters_pred = 5,
  nterms_max = 2,
  seed = 46782345
)
```

Notes:

(1) In principle, the output from na.fail() could be assigned back to the
    original object (i.e., `d_test <- lapply([...])`), but this is not done
    here to avoid a bug in case na.fail() gets replaced by some other NA
    handler (e.g., na.omit()) in the future (because at least for na.omit()
    and na.exclude(), `d_test <- lapply([...])` would be incorrect, as
    `d_test` consists of different elements).
(2) Furthermore, we iterate over `d_test`'s names (not `d_test`'s elements
    themselves) in order to have a slightly more informative error message.
(3) Furthermore, elements `y` and `y_oscale` are not checked for `NA`s because
    at least `y` may be only-`NA`s in case of the latent projection (and in
    case of the latent projection, some features of projpred might work also
    if `y_oscale` is only-`NA`s; PSIS-LOO CV will not work, though).

model size.

Fixes for argument `nterms` of `proj_helper()` (#110)

* In proj_helper(): `list(...)$nterms` is always `NULL` as there is a predefined argument `nterms`.

* Fix a bug for calls like
```r
mylinpred <- proj_linpred(project(myfit,
                                  solution_terms = c("V3")),
                          nterms = 2)
```
which previously raised an error (but should work without raising an error) and for calls like
```r
mylinpred <- proj_linpred(project(myfit,
                                  solution_terms = c("V3")),
                          nterms = 1)
```
which previously did not raise an error (but should raise an error).

* Fix what is probably a precedence typo, see `?Syntax`.

* In proj_helper(): Use `count_terms_chosen(x$solution_terms)` instead of `(length(x$solution_terms) + 1)` to be better prepared for no-intercept models.

* Argument `nterms` in proj_helper() is passed to project(), so it doesn't match the output of count_terms_chosen() (since count_terms_chosen() counts the intercept but argument `nterms` of project() does not). Therefore, add +1 to `nterms` (if specified). This also affects the behavior of `nterms` in the case `inherits(object, "projection") || (length(object) > 0 && inherits(object[[1]], "projection"))`, i.e. when `nterms` is used to filter `object`.

* Do not use `nterms` in the case `inherits(object, "projection") || (length(object) > 0 && inherits(object[[1]], "projection"))`, i.e. do not use `nterms` to filter `object` if it results from project() (filtering wasn't possible before commit 8909d38e372f5945364d6083d33a02856555cf32 anyway).

```r
dat_gauss <- data.frame(y = df_gaussian$y, df_gaussian$x)
fit <- rstanarm::stan_glm(
  y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5, family = gaussian(), data = dat_gauss,
  QR = TRUE, chains = 1, iter = 500, warmup = 499, refresh = 0, seed = 9876
)
stopifnot(nrow(as.matrix(fit)) == 1)
extractor_cust <- function(object, newdata, wrhs = NULL, orhs = NULL,
                           extract_y = TRUE) {
  return(y_wobs_offs(newdata = newdata, wrhs = wrhs, orhs = orhs,
                     resp_form = if (extract_y) ~ y else NULL))
}
ref_cust <- init_refmodel(
  fit,
  data = dat_gauss,
  formula = y ~ X6 + X7,
  family = gaussian(),
  extract_model_data = extractor_cust,
  cvfun = function(folds) {
    kfold(
      fit, K = max(folds), save_fits = TRUE, folds = folds, cores = 1
    )$fits[, "fit"]
  },
  dis = as.matrix(fit)[, "sigma"],
  cvrefbuilder = function(cvfit) {
    init_refmodel(cvfit,
                  data = dat_gauss[-cvfit$omitted, , drop = FALSE],
                  formula = y ~ X6 + X7,
                  family = gaussian(),
                  extract_model_data = extractor_cust,
                  dis = as.matrix(cvfit)[, "sigma"],
                  called_from_cvrefbuilder = TRUE)
  }
)
pr_ref <- predict(ref_cust, type = "link")

)
pr_ref_lat <- predict(ref_cust_lat)

On Windows, some special handling is needed:

This commit basically reverts the following commits (in the order from top to
bottom):

"Simplify the handling of `...` and `dot_args` as much as possible."
"Further enhance `.noexport`."
"Enhance `.noexport`."
"Add a comment for `.options.snow`."

The reason for the revert of (most of) commit
"Simplify the handling of `...` and `dot_args` as much as possible."
is that on Windows, the 'doParallel' backend complains about incorrect `...`
usage when using the simplified (implicit) `...` code. Instead, the 'doParallel'
backend seems to require `dot_args <- list(...)` to be defined explicitly.

The reason for the revert of commits
"Further enhance `.noexport`."
"Enhance `.noexport`."
(some minor no-op modifications have been performed, too) is that on Windows,
the 'doParallel' package can't find object `refmodel` if it is listed in
`.noexport` (and the same would happen with `y_wobs_test`).

The reason for the revert of commit
"Add a comment for `.options.snow`."
is that I probably misunderstood the implications of `attachExportEnv = TRUE`:
Here, "attaching" is probably the R term as in "attaching a package". So it
shouldn't affect the runtime (at least not heavily).

Also note that on Windows, the 'doParallel' backend would allow `.export` to be
omitted, but the 'doFuture' backend requires `.export` to be specified (at least
when using the 'callr' plan for package 'future').

Filter column indices of sparse matrix to ensure non-negativity (#576)

In Issue #573, I observed that `scipy`s compressed sparse column matrix
was throwing an exception about specification of negative indices. I
traced this issue to the column specification in the C++ implementation
of RMTB.

I could not figure out what precisely was going wrong. However, by
simply replacing all negative column indices with zeros, I found that
the unit tests pass. This is in no way a permanent solution, but given
the lack of shared understanding of this code, it is preferable to it
being fully nonfunctional.

While we're at it, replace all internal `int`s by `long` in order to
support larger model sizes, similar to the diff made in RMTC.

Filter column indices of sparse matrix to ensure non-negativity

In Issue #573, I observed that `scipy`s compressed sparse column matrix
was throwing an exception about specification of negative indices. I
traced this issue to the column specification in the C++ implementation
of RMTB.

I could not figure out what precisely was going wrong. However, by
simply replacing all negative column indices with zeros, I found that
the unit tests pass. This is in no way a permanent solution, but given
the lack of shared understanding of this code, it is preferable to it
being fully nonfunctional.

While we're at it, replace all internal `int`s by `long` in order to
support larger model sizes, similar to the diff made in RMTC.
